method: Official websites fetched directly on 2026-11-18 for offerings, seasons and prices; coordinates from OpenStreetMap Nominatim or Wikipedia; images from the Wikimedia Commons API. See RESEARCH_SOURCES.md.

experiences.name: Canada Agriculture and Food Museum
experiences.community: Federal agricultural research tradition of the Central Experimental Farm
experiences.short_description: A working farm and food-science museum inside Ottawa's Central Experimental Farm.
experiences.description: Visit the livestock barns to see cattle, horses, goats and alpacas. Indoor exhibits cover food science and sustainable farming, and the kitchen runs seasonal cooking demonstrations. The museum is open year-round.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The museum sits on the Central Experimental Farm, founded in 1886 to study crops and livestock suited to Canada. Exhibits cover farming, aquaculture and food production.
experiences.cultural_context: The federal government set up the Experimental Farm system in the late 1800s as settlement expanded west. Ingenium offers free admission to Indigenous visitors.

food_spotlight.name: Demonstration Kitchen harvest demos
food_spotlight.description: Seasonal demonstrations use crops such as apples and sweet corn to show how farm products become food.

activities: Watch animal care and farm demonstrations
experiences.season_notes: Open Wednesday to Sunday, 9 a.m.-5 p.m., year-round (closed Dec. 25-26). Free admission daily from 4-5 p.m.

pricing.notes: Regular adult fee, taxes not included; youth 3-17 $12.75; children 2 and under free; family $42.50. Parking extra.

experiences.name: Mādahòkì Farm
experiences.community: Indigenous Experiences; on unceded Algonquin territory; name is Anishinaabemowin
experiences.short_description: An Indigenous-run agritourism farm in Ottawa's Greenbelt, home to a herd of endangered Ojibwe Spirit Horses.
experiences.description: Meet Ojibwe Spirit Horses and other farm animals. The Legacy Trail introduces traditional medicines and the Seven Grandfather Teachings. Shop at the Indigenous marketplace or book the Trail of the Spirit Horse.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The farm helps rebuild the Ojibwe Spirit Horse population. Its programs teach animal care, plant knowledge and food traditions.
experiences.cultural_context: Mādahòkì means 'to share the land' in Anishinaabemowin. The farm opened in 2021 on unceded Algonquin territory and hosts the Summer Solstice Indigenous Festival and Sìgwan.

food_spotlight.name: Indigenous snack bar and Bannock in a Bag
food_spotlight.description: A rotating snack bar serves Indigenous treats during the visitor season, and the farm sells its own bannock mix in the marketplace.

activities: Trail of the Spirit Horse self-guided experience (paid)
experiences.season_notes: 2026 visitor experiences ran July 9 - October 4 (Thursday-Sunday, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. for add-ons). The marketplace is open Thursday-Sunday, 11 a.m.-4 p.m.; holiday programming is also offered.

pricing.notes: General admission is free. Paid add-ons: Trail of the Spirit Horse $20 adult / $12 child under 12 (approx. 45 min); workshops and horse encounters are extra.

experiences.name: Upper Canada Village
experiences.community: Loyalist and English-Canadian settlers of the St. Lawrence valley
experiences.short_description: A living-history village recreating rural English Canada in 1866, with working mills and heritage trades.
experiences.description: Explore more than 40 historic buildings. Watch millers grind flour, see blacksmiths at work or eat at Willard's Hotel. PumpkInferno and Alight at Night run outside the main season.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The village shows the farm-to-table chain of a nineteenth-century Ontario community, from field and mill to bakery and table. Working mills and farm buildings demonstrate how grain, wool and dairy sustained rural households.
experiences.cultural_context: The village depicts life in 1866 along the St. Lawrence, where Loyalist and other English-speaking settlers lived. Many buildings came from villages flooded by the Seaway project.

food_spotlight.name: Village bread and cheddar
food_spotlight.description: The Village Café serves grilled cheddar sandwiches on fresh-baked Village Bread, and Willard's Hotel offers period-style dishes such as rarebit and afternoon tea.

activities: Watch the working mills and heritage trades
experiences.season_notes: Main daytime season runs roughly May to September (exact 2027 dates not yet published). PumpkInferno runs in October and Alight at Night on select nights Nov. 27, 2026 - Jan. 2, 2027.

pricing.notes: Main-season adult (25-64) $26 plus HST; youth 5-12 $17; under 5 free; family $80. Special events priced separately.

experiences.name: Sucrerie de la Montagne
experiences.community: Québécois maple-sugaring tradition
experiences.short_description: A traditional wood-fired sugar shack in a maple forest west of Montreal, famous for its sugaring-off feasts.
experiences.description: See maple sap collected in pails and boiled over a wood fire during sugaring season. Try a sugar-shack meal and maple taffy on snow. Meals and overnight stays are available by reservation outside the sugar season.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Maple syrup production is one of Quebec's signature agricultural traditions, and the sucrerie demonstrates the older, labour-intensive pail-and-wood-fire method. Its menu showcases farm staples such as pea soup, ham, baked beans and maple desserts.
experiences.cultural_context: Founded in 1978 by Pierre Faucher and now run with his son Stefan, the sucrerie presents the 'temps des sucres' as a festive rural Québécois gathering. It describes itself as a recognized Québec heritage site.

food_spotlight.name: Repas de cabane à sucre
food_spotlight.description: A multi-course meal of pea soup, maple-smoked ham, wood-fired baked beans, Beauce-style meat pie and sugar pie, plus taffy on snow.

activities: Visit the wood-fired evaporator and maple bush
Horse-drawn rides and live music (group minimums apply)
experiences.season_notes: Sugaring-off season with taffy on snow runs February to April (2026 rates listed Feb. 21 - May 3). Meals and lodging are available year-round by reservation.

pricing.notes: 2026 rates: 13+ lunch $58-63 depending on date and day; ages 7-12 $31; ages 3-6 $26; taxes extra; reservation required. Price is for the meal experience.

experiences.name: Fromagerie La Station
experiences.community: Multi-generation family farm in the Eastern Townships (Cantons-de-l'Est)
experiences.short_description: An organic family dairy farm in Compton that makes raw-milk farmhouse cheeses and runs an ÉCONOMUSÉE of farm cheesemaking.
experiences.description: Follow a free, year-round route through exhibits about the farm and its ripening rooms. Book a guided tour to see the hay dryer and pastured cows and try the cheeses. The shop sells Alfred Le Fermier and Comtomme.
experiences.agricultural_significance: La Station is a certified-organic farm where cheese is made from the herd's own milk, so pasture, cows and cheese are part of one operation. It shows how farmstead cheesemaking adds value to dairy farming in the Coaticook region.
experiences.cultural_context: The farm presents itself as the work of four generations of farmers. It belongs to Quebec's farmhouse-cheese revival and to the ÉCONOMUSÉE network, which showcases traditional crafts in working businesses.

food_spotlight.name: Alfred Le Fermier
food_spotlight.description: One of the farm's signature cheeses, made from the farm's own organic milk.

activities: Guided farm and cheese-dairy tour with tasting
See cows on pasture and the hay dryer
experiences.season_notes: The self-guided route is open year-round during shop hours, including winter. Guided tours run on dates listed in the online booking system.

pricing.notes: Guided tour $18 per adult, tasting included; children 12 and under free. Self-guided route has no charge.

experiences.name: Abbaye de Saint-Benoît-du-Lac
experiences.community: Benedictine monks (founded from the French abbey of Saint-Wandrille)
experiences.short_description: A Benedictine abbey on Lake Memphremagog where monks make award-winning cheeses and visitors pick apples in the abbey orchards.
experiences.description: Visit the church for Gregorian chant or buy cheese, cider and preserves made by the monks. Guided tours run in summer and the orchard opens for apple picking on early autumn weekends.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The monks run a cheese dairy supplied entirely by local dairy farms, producing cheeses such as Bleu Bénédictin, and they tend extensive apple orchards used for fresh fruit and cider. Their products carry the PAX mark, which certifies work done by monks.
experiences.cultural_context: The community traces its origins to monks of the abbey of Saint-Wandrille in Normandy who, exiled by French anti-clerical laws, settled on Lake Memphremagog in 1912. The current abbey church, designed by Dan Hanganu, was built between 1990 and 1994.

food_spotlight.name: Bleu Bénédictin
food_spotlight.description: A creamy blue-veined cheese made by the monks and a repeated prize-winner at the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair.

activities: Shop monastery cheeses, ciders and compotes
experiences.season_notes: Shop open daily year-round (9 a.m.-6 p.m. June-October, 9 a.m.-5 p.m. November-May). Orchards open weekends from early September to Thanksgiving; guided tours mainly late June to early September.

pricing.notes: Guided tour: $15 adult, $9 ages 7-17, free 6 and under, $35 family. Visiting the shop and church is free; apples are sold by weight.

experiences.name: Sainte-Marie among the Hurons
experiences.community: 17th-century French Jesuit mission in Wendake, homeland of the Wendat Nation
experiences.short_description: A reconstructed 1639 French Jesuit mission in Wendat country, with a heritage farm of 17th-century crops and animal breeds.
experiences.description: Try quill writing, lacrosse or canoeing at the reconstructed fort. The heritage farm is open from early May to Thanksgiving and keeps breeds such as Canadienne cattle and Houdan chickens.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The farm interprets the crops and animals that sustained life in Wendake in the 1600s, including Canadienne cattle, Canada's original dairy breed, of which fewer than 200 are registered. It also highlights the Wendat as skilled farmers whose agriculture supported the region.
experiences.cultural_context: Wendake, on Georgian Bay, is the ancestral homeland of the Wendat, a matrilineal farming and trading people. French Jesuits built their mission headquarters here in the 1600s. The province runs the reconstructed site.

food_spotlight.name: Restaurant Sainte-Marie
food_spotlight.description: The on-site restaurant is open year-round; harvest events such as Hearth to Table focus on historic foodways.

activities: Explore the reconstructed mission with interpreters
Visit the heritage farm and gardens
experiences.season_notes: Daily operation resumes May 1, 2027; the heritage farm is open early May to Thanksgiving. Special events (e.g., First Light, Nov. 26 - Dec. 13) and the restaurant operate outside the season.

pricing.notes: DEMO ESTIMATE: regular daily admission was not published during the off-season. Published event admission is $15 tax-included; a season pass is $35. Indigenous persons admitted free.

experiences.name: Doon Heritage Village
experiences.community: Waterloo Region settler communities, including Old Order Mennonites (Pennsylvania German heritage)
experiences.short_description: A 60-acre living-history village showing rural Waterloo Region in 1914, with heritage farm animals.
experiences.description: Step into 1914 in the village's homes, shops and farm buildings. See farm animals in season or try Taste of 1914 on Saturday afternoons. Admission includes the adjoining Ken Seiling Waterloo Region Museum.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The village interprets the farm economy of Waterloo Region on the eve of the First World War, when mixed family farms supplied local markets. Seasonal livestock come from area farms, linking the museum to present-day agriculture.
experiences.cultural_context: Pennsylvania German Mennonites and later German immigrants settled in Waterloo Region. Old Order Mennonites, including descendants of Peter Martin, helped restore his 1820 house.

food_spotlight.name: Taste of 1914
food_spotlight.description: A Saturday-afternoon program presenting foods of the period in the village.

activities: Walk the 1914 village with costumed interpreters
experiences.season_notes: Village season runs from early spring to Labour Day, plus select fall Saturdays and Thanksgiving weekend (farm animals leave at the end of summer). The museum galleries are open year-round, Wednesday-Sunday.

pricing.notes: Adult (18-54) $15 plus HST; children 5-12 $8; under 5 free; family/small group (4) $30. Includes museum galleries.

image.author: Pcorb
image.caption: Doon Heritage Village, Kitchener

experiences.name: Orwell Corner Historic Village
experiences.community: Rural Prince Edward Island settler community of the 1890s
experiences.short_description: A restored 1890s Island crossroads village with a working farm, agricultural museum and tea room.
experiences.description: Feed farm animals, take a wagon ride and visit the village blacksmith and general store. The Agricultural Museum displays farm equipment. Summer visitors can eat at the tea room or book a bread- and butter-making program.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Orwell Corner preserves the mixed-farming way of life that defined rural PEI, where families raised livestock and crops for their own tables and local trade. Its agricultural museum and working barnyard make that history tangible.
experiences.cultural_context: The village is operated by the PEI Museum and Heritage Foundation and depicts a late-Victorian Island farm community in the 1890s. Its gardens and picnic area overlook Orwell Bay.

food_spotlight.name: Food on the Farm
food_spotlight.description: A paid program in which participants make bread and butter the old-fashioned way; village admission is included.

experiences.season_notes: Summer season only; the village was closed for the season at research time and 2027 dates were not yet published (months listed are approximate). Tea room open 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. daily in summer, cash only.

pricing.notes: Standard village admission was not published at research time. Food on the Farm and Forge programs are $50 per person and 'In the Time of Maud' is $60, each including admission.

experiences.name: Ross Farm Museum
experiences.community: Irish-born Captain William Ross and disbanded soldiers of the Nova Scotia Fencibles (settled 1816)
experiences.short_description: A 60-acre living-history farm showing Nova Scotia family farming more than a century ago, complete with working oxen.
experiences.description: Meet heritage animals and watch interpreters demonstrate farm chores. Rosebank Cottage often has samples of traditional recipes. Year-round workshops include ox handling, spoon carving and sewing.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Ross Farm preserves heritage livestock and the ox-powered farming methods that cleared and worked Nova Scotia's forested interior. Its beginner ox workshops keep a rare draft-animal skill alive.
experiences.cultural_context: Captain William Ross moved here from Ireland in 1816 with his family and a group of disbanded soldiers. Rosebank, the house he built the following year, still stands.

food_spotlight.name: Rosebank Cottage recipes
food_spotlight.description: Traditional recipes are frequently sampled in Rosebank Cottage during visits.

experiences.season_notes: Open year-round with hours that vary by season; at research time the museum was open Saturday-Sunday 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Workshops are scheduled through the year.

pricing.notes: Adult $15; child 6-17 $5; 5 and under free; family $30.

experiences.name: Grand-Pré National Historic Site
experiences.community: Acadians; on the unceded territory of the Mi'kmaq
experiences.short_description: The heart of the UNESCO-listed Landscape of Grand-Pré, where Acadian dykelands still produce farmland reclaimed from the sea.
experiences.description: Learn about Acadian settlement and the Deportation at the visitor centre, then visit the Memorial Church and garden. Parks Canada offers guided tours. The Harvest Moon Trail passes through the surrounding farmland.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Acadian farmers drained tidal marshes with dykes and wooden sluices called aboiteaux. Farmers still work the dykelands, part of a 1,300-hectare UNESCO World Heritage Site.
experiences.cultural_context: Grand-Pré is a monument to Acadian culture and to the Deportation of the Acadians that began in 1755. Parks Canada and the Mi'kmaq of Nova Scotia co-manage protected areas under the Toqi'maliaptmu'k Arrangement, recognizing the site's location on unceded Mi'kmaw territory.

food_spotlight.name: Dykeland harvests
food_spotlight.description: The reclaimed marshlands around the site remain working farmland; the site itself does not operate a food program.

activities: Guided tour with a Parks Canada interpreter
Walk or cycle the Harvest Moon trail
experiences.season_notes: Visitor Reception Centre and Memorial Church open May 15 - Oct. 12 (2026), 9 a.m.-5 p.m. Grounds and garden are accessible year-round.

pricing.notes: Daily adult admission $10 (May-October); senior $8.50; youth 17 and under free. Guided tour $6.50 per person extra.

experiences.name: Kings Landing
experiences.community: Rural settler communities of the Saint John River valley
experiences.short_description: A living-history settlement on the Saint John River that recreates 19th-century rural New Brunswick.
experiences.description: Visit farms and workshops in a riverside village about 20 minutes west of Fredericton. Watch interpreters demonstrate trades or eat at the King's Head Inn. Holiday dinners and a Christmas village run outside summer.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Kings Landing shows how river-valley farms fed New Brunswick households about 200 years ago. Interpreters demonstrate the farm work, food preparation and trades that kept a rural community self-sufficient.
experiences.cultural_context: The settlement represents the English-speaking rural communities of the Saint John River valley in the 19th century. Kings Landing offers free admission to Indigenous visitors and to military veterans and serving members.

food_spotlight.name: King's Head Inn
food_spotlight.description: A historical-setting dining room serving hearty meals and treats; holiday feasts are offered in winter.

activities: Watch heritage farming and trades demonstrations
Dine at the King's Head Inn
experiences.season_notes: Main season June to October (2026 season began June 6); special Christmas events from late November.

pricing.notes: 2026 general admission, tax included: adult 19-64 $19.55; youth 6-18 $16.62; 5 and under free; family $60.

experiences.name: Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Village
experiences.community: Ukrainian Canadian settlers of east-central Alberta
experiences.short_description: An open-air museum where costumed interpreters tell the stories of Ukrainian pioneers on the Alberta prairie.
experiences.description: Visit a historic school, railway station and blacksmith shop. Costumed interpreters tell the stories of Ukrainian settlers in east-central Alberta. Special events run in summer.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Ukrainian immigrants homesteaded the parkland east of Edmonton and built farming communities there. The village shows the rural buildings and work of those early settlers.
experiences.cultural_context: The village, run by the Government of Alberta, tells the first-hand stories of early settlers in east-central Alberta, an area closely linked to Ukrainian immigration. It sits 25 minutes east of Edmonton on Highway 16.
experiences.season_notes: Closed Sept. 14, 2026 - May 21, 2027; the summer season runs from late May to mid-September.

pricing.notes: Adult (18-64) $18; youth 7-17 $11; child 0-6 free; family $45.

experiences.name: Fort Edmonton Park
experiences.community: First Nations and Métis Peoples of the region (partner: Confederacy of Treaty Six First Nations and Métis Nation of Alberta)
experiences.short_description: A living-history park in Edmonton's river valley whose Indigenous Peoples Experience stays open on winter weekends.
experiences.description: Take a train or streetcar through recreations of Edmonton's past. The Indigenous Peoples Experience shares First Nations and Métis histories and runs workshops on winter weekends. Allow at least four hours in summer.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The park traces the shift from the fur-trade fort economy to the farms and settler towns that grew around Edmonton. Animal rides and historic farm buildings illustrate prairie livelihoods.
experiences.cultural_context: Fort Edmonton Park formally partners with the Confederacy of Treaty Six First Nations and the Métis Nation of Alberta and offers free admission to Indigenous Peoples. Its later-era streets interpret settlement by newcomers from many backgrounds.

food_spotlight.name: Indigenous Peoples Experience workshops
food_spotlight.description: Feature workshops such as sealskin crafting are offered in winter; the park's food outlets operate in the summer season.

experiences.season_notes: Full park open in the summer season (2027 dates not yet published). From Sept. 26, 2026 to Apr. 25, 2027 only the Indigenous Peoples Experience is open, Saturdays and Sundays 12-4 p.m.

pricing.notes: Fall/winter Indigenous Peoples Experience admission: adult $20, child/youth 3-17 $12, family $50. Summer full-park admission was not published at research time; pony and wagon rides $8 each.

experiences.name: Mennonite Heritage Village
experiences.community: Russian Mennonite settlers of southern Manitoba
experiences.short_description: A living-history village and museum telling the story of the Russian Mennonites who settled southern Manitoba.
experiences.description: See a working windmill, a Chortitz housebarn and indoor exhibits on Mennonite history. The Livery Barn Restaurant serves traditional dishes in summer. The galleries stay open year-round.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Mennonite settlers farmed southern Manitoba in compact villages, and the housebarn, which joined family home and livestock barn under one roof, shows how they adapted to the prairie. The windmill demonstrates the wind-powered grain milling that served those communities.
experiences.cultural_context: The village focuses on Russian Mennonites, a German-speaking Anabaptist people who emigrated from the Russian Empire to the Steinbach area. Exhibits and memorials also address conscientious objection and the persecution of Mennonites who stayed in the Soviet Union.

food_spotlight.name: Peppernuts and Livery Barn Restaurant
food_spotlight.description: Small spiced peppernut cookies are sold at the General Store, and the Livery Barn Restaurant serves Mennonite-style meals in summer.

activities: Tour the historic village and windmill
experiences.season_notes: Summer season May 1 - Sept. 30 (village, restaurant and store open daily). Oct. 1 - Apr. 30 the museum galleries are open Tuesday-Saturday and heritage buildings are closed.

pricing.notes: Summer admission: adult $16; children 6-12 $9; 5 and under free; family $55. Winter adult admission $8.

experiences.name: Wanuskewin Heritage Park
experiences.community: Northern Plains Indigenous peoples (name is nēhiyawēwin / Plains Cree)
experiences.short_description: A sacred gathering place of more than 6,400 years north of Saskatoon, with a conservation bison herd and Indigenous cuisine.
experiences.description: Walk through restored grassland and see the plains bison herd. Visit the galleries or join a drop-in program. Weekend performances may feature dance, drumming or fiddle music.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Northern Plains peoples gathered here for thousands of years to hunt bison and harvest plants. The park is restoring the grasslands and has brought bison back.
experiences.cultural_context: The name, from nēhiyawēwin (Plains Cree), is roughly translated as 'seeking peace of mind'. The park works to advance understanding of the evolving cultures of Northern Plains Indigenous peoples and reinvests admission fees in programming, grassland restoration and its bison herd.

food_spotlight.name: Indigenous cuisine at the Wanuskewin restaurant
food_spotlight.description: The on-site restaurant serves a taste of Indigenous cuisine (11 a.m.-4 p.m.).

experiences.season_notes: Open year-round, daily 9:30 a.m.-5 p.m.; closed fall/winter statutory holidays.

pricing.notes: 2026 rates: adult 18-64 $16; child 6-17 $8; 0-5 free; family (up to 6) $40. Parking $5.

experiences.name: Motherwell Homestead National Historic Site
experiences.address: Lanark Place homestead, south of Abernethy
experiences.community: Ontario-born pioneer farmers of the Qu'Appelle region
experiences.short_description: The restored prairie homestead of W.R. Motherwell, a pioneer farmer who became Canada's Minister of Agriculture.
experiences.description: Explore W. R. Motherwell's prairie homestead about an hour east of Regina. Parks Canada offers tours, a children's day camp and a fall pumpkin harvest festival.
experiences.agricultural_significance: William Richard Motherwell promoted dryland farming and later served as federal Minister of Agriculture. The homestead shows how farmers grew grain in Saskatchewan's dry climate.
experiences.cultural_context: Parks Canada notes that the fertile Qu'Appelle region was a crossroads for First Nations, Métis and waves of newcomers. Motherwell was part of the late-19th-century stream of pioneer farmers who moved west from Ontario.

food_spotlight.name: Pumpkin Harvest Festival
food_spotlight.description: A family fall festival celebrating the harvest on the homestead.

experiences.season_notes: Seasonal; the site was closed for the season at research time and 2027 dates were not yet published (months listed are approximate, with a fall pumpkin festival).

pricing.notes: Daily adult $10; senior $8.50; youth 17 and under free. Enhanced programs extra (e.g., Little Red Hen $41.75).

experiences.name: Nk'Mip Cellars
experiences.community: Osoyoos Indian Band (Syilx / Okanagan)
experiences.short_description: North America's first Indigenous-owned and -operated winery, set in vineyards above Osoyoos Lake.
experiences.description: Try a walk-in tasting of the Winemaker's Series or Qwam Qwmt wines. Book a seasonal food pairing, eat on the Sweetgrass patio or visit the neighbouring Nk'Mip Desert Cultural Centre.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The Osoyoos Indian Band grows grapes for VQA wines in the hot, dry south Okanagan.
experiences.cultural_context: The winery sits on Osoyoos Indian Band land in the south Okanagan. Nk'Mip means 'bottomland' and Qwam Qwmt means 'achieving excellence'.

food_spotlight.name: Sip & Soups pairing
food_spotlight.description: A reserved fall experience pairing three Nk'Mip wines with three of the chef's soups ($25).

experiences.season_notes: Wine shop and tasting room open daily 10 a.m.-5 p.m. year-round, except listed holiday closures (Dec. 24-26, Jan. 1).

pricing.notes: Fall tasting flight $5 per person (non-redeemable); Sip & Soups pairing $25. Tastings are for adults of legal drinking age.

experiences.name: Father Pandosy Mission Heritage Site
experiences.community: French Oblate missionaries (Oblates of Mary Immaculate)
experiences.short_description: The 1859 Oblate mission that was the first permanent non-Indigenous settlement in the Okanagan Valley.
experiences.description: See the original chapel, root house and Brothers' House at this four-acre site on Kelowna's Benvoulin Road. The grounds are open from dawn to dusk in season.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Father Charles Pandosy and the Oblates farmed the mission, raising hogs, sheep, oats, barley, wheat, tobacco and potatoes and irrigating their fields. The surviving root house reflects the food storage that kept a self-sufficient mission going.
experiences.cultural_context: French-born Oblate priest Charles Pandosy founded the mission in 1859, and the site is recognized as the impetus for later settlement of the Okanagan. It is a designated provincial heritage site jointly administered by the Okanagan Historical Society and the Roman Catholic Bishop of Nelson.

food_spotlight.name: Mission root house
food_spotlight.description: An original 1859-era root house used to store the mission's harvest.

activities: Self-guided tour of the heritage buildings
See the original chapel and root house
experiences.season_notes: Grounds open dawn to dusk from Easter to Thanksgiving, according to the Okanagan Historical Society.

pricing.notes: Suggested donation of $2 per person toward site upkeep.

experiences.name: Kilby Historic Site
experiences.community: Kilby family and early-20th-century settlers of Harrison Mills
experiences.short_description: BC's 'museum of rural life', with a 1906 general store and a 1920s-style working farm in the Fraser Valley.
experiences.description: Explore the 1906 Kilby General Store and feed animals at Waterloo Farm. The café serves seasonal food made with regional ingredients. There's a riverside campground next door.
experiences.agricultural_significance: In 1912 the Kilby family started the Waterloo Jersey Dairy Farm on more than 200 acres beside their store, also raising chickens and pigs. The preserved farm shows how livestock gave early Fraser Valley settlers both food and income.
experiences.cultural_context: Harrison Mills was a boom-and-bust river community, and the Kilby site is its only remaining trace. The farm was named after Thomas Kilby's first Canadian home in Waterloo, Ontario; the family's earlier origins are not documented in the sources consulted.

food_spotlight.name: Kilby Café seasonal menu
food_spotlight.description: The café runs seasonal menus, such as a fall 'Taste the Wild' event with elk bannock tacos and salmon chowder.

activities: Feed animals on the Waterloo Farm
experiences.season_notes: 2026: Apr. 2 - Dec. 13, with days varying by season (Thursday-Monday in summer, weekends Nov.-Dec.). Closed mid-December to spring.

pricing.notes: Adult $16; youth 6-16 / students $11; 5 and under free; family (2+2) $42.

experiences.name: Gulf of Georgia Cannery National Historic Site
experiences.community: Japanese, Chinese and European cannery workers alongside First Nations workers
experiences.short_description: An 1894 salmon cannery in Steveston village that tells the story of Canada's West Coast fishing industry.
experiences.description: Follow the old salmon canning line and see the herring reduction plant. Exhibits cover cannery work and Indigenous women's connections to fishing in the Salish Sea. Steveston remains a working fishing village.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Salmon canning was one of British Columbia's largest employers and export industries, and this plant, nicknamed the 'Monster Cannery', packed more than 2.5 million cans in 1897. It shows how wild fisheries fed a global food trade.
experiences.cultural_context: Each canning season drew hundreds of workers, usually of First Nations, Chinese, Japanese and European descent, making the cannery a meeting point of BC's immigrant and Indigenous communities. The site is operated by the Gulf of Georgia Cannery Society on behalf of Parks Canada.

food_spotlight.name: Canned Fraser River salmon
food_spotlight.description: The exhibits trace how salmon went from boat to can; food is not served inside the museum.

experiences.season_notes: Open daily 10 a.m.-5 p.m. year-round, closed on listed statutory holidays. The building is colder than outdoors; dress warmly.

pricing.notes: Adult $14.75; senior $12.50; youth 17 and under free.

experiences.name: Dänojà Zho Cultural Centre
experiences.community: Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in (Hän-speaking First Nation)
experiences.short_description: The Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in cultural centre on Dawson's waterfront, gateway to Hän heritage and the river life of the Klondike.
experiences.description: See the Gathering Room's summer exhibit or join a river walk. The shop sells clothing, beadwork, jewellery, music and books by First Nations artists. The centre looks across the Yukon River toward Moosehide Village.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The centre's architecture draws on salmon drying racks and winter shelters, reflecting a food system built on river fishing and harvesting. Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in also operate TH Farm near Dawson, described as the only First Nations working farm north of 60.
experiences.cultural_context: Dänojà Zho means 'Long Ago House'. It opened in July 1998 to give the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in a strong presence in their traditional territory that would not be bound to the gold-rush story, and its design won the Lieutenant Governor of BC's Medal in Architecture.

food_spotlight.name: Yukon River salmon traditions
food_spotlight.description: Salmon drying racks inspire the building's design; the centre does not list a food service.

activities: Summer exhibitions in the Gathering Room
experiences.season_notes: Visitor programs run May to September; the building is open year-round for community use and rentals.

pricing.notes: Admission price was not published on the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in page at research time.

experiences.name: Dawson City Farmers' Market
experiences.community: Klondike growers and artisans (multicultural community of Dawson City)
experiences.short_description: A summer weekend market where Klondike farmers sell plants, vegetables, berries and preserves under the midnight sun.
experiences.description: Shop at Waterfront Park on summer weekends. Look for bedding plants early in the season and vegetables, berries and preserves later on. An artists' market runs alongside it.
experiences.agricultural_significance: The Klondike valley has some of the Yukon's best growing conditions, and the market is the main outlet for the small farms that supply Dawson. It shows how northern growers use long summer daylight to raise crops far north.
experiences.cultural_context: Market gardens fed Dawson during the gold rush. Today local farms, including the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in teaching farm, supply Dawson's markets. The artists' market uses a Hän name.

food_spotlight.name: Klondike-grown produce
food_spotlight.description: Seasonal vegetables, herbs, berries, apples and preserves grown in the Klondike valley.

activities: Buy bedding plants and nursery stock
experiences.season_notes: Saturdays and Sundays, mid-May to mid-September; farmers' market 11 a.m.-4 p.m., artists' market 11 a.m.-3 p.m.

pricing.notes: Free to browse; goods priced by vendors.

experiences.name: Rockpile Remedies
experiences.community: Klondike Gold Rush landscape, reclaimed by present-day Dawson growers
experiences.short_description: Herb gardens built on reclaimed Gold Rush dredge tailings, with garden tours and herbal-remedy workshops.
experiences.description: See how herbs grow in quartz-rock beds on old dredge tailings. Make an herbal remedy in a workshop or shop for Yukon-grown products. The farm also offers wildcrafting and herbalism courses.
experiences.agricultural_significance: Herbs grow in beds made from quartz tailings left by gold dredging. The gardens show how cultivation can reclaim disturbed ground in the subarctic.
experiences.cultural_context: The tailings came from industrial dredging after the Klondike Gold Rush. Tours cover that history and how the gardens are used for herbal medicine today.

food_spotlight.name: Yukon-grown herbal remedies
food_spotlight.description: Workshop participants make their own herbal remedy from plants grown on site.

activities: Guided garden tour on reclaimed tailings
experiences.season_notes: Summer season May 27 - Sept. 27, Monday-Friday 10 a.m.-5 p.m. (Saturdays at the Dawson Farmers' Market). Winter shop hours October-April by appointment/limited days.

pricing.notes: Tour price not listed on the Travel Yukon profile; booking through the operator.

experiences.name: Inuvik Community Greenhouse
experiences.community: Inuvik residents in the Gwich'in Settlement Area and Inuvialuit region (community-run, not specific to one Nation)
experiences.short_description: North America's northernmost commercial greenhouse, a converted hockey arena growing food under the midnight sun.
experiences.description: Summer tours visit community garden plots, including beds for Elders, children and the food bank. The café changes its menu weekly based on the harvest. The greenhouse also sells plants.
experiences.agricultural_significance: North of the Arctic Circle, the greenhouse uses summer daylight to grow fresh produce locally and reduce reliance on shipped food.
experiences.cultural_context: Gwich'in, Inuvialuit and other Inuvik residents rent plots and volunteer at the greenhouse.

food_spotlight.name: Inuvik Greenhouse Café
food_spotlight.description: A garden-inspired menu that changes weekly to use the greenhouse's harvest.

experiences.season_notes: Scheduled tours June through September. Café open June-August (Wed 5-8 p.m., Thu-Sun 10 a.m.-4 p.m.) and September weekends.

pricing.notes: No current tour price published by the Town of Inuvik or NWT Tourism.
